speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon. Sir GEORGE PERLEY (Acting Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That pursuant to the provisions of the Canadian Radio Act, 1932, the House of Commons hereby approves the purchase of the radio broadcasting stations and equipment of the Canadian National Railways by the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Commission for the sum of $50,000.
He said: In explanation I may say that this is a formal motion which is considered necessary as subsection (b) of section 9 of the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act, 1932, provides that the commission shall have power, among other things to acquire existing private stations by purchase, subject to the approval of parliament.
His Excellency the Governor General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution approves of the same, and recommends it to the favourable consideration of the house.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.

Mr. MANION; The proposal for the acquisition by the radio commission of these stations was not made at all by the government. The directors of the Canadian National Railways dealt with the matter and decided that the railways should get out of the radio business inasmuch as it was costing them $80,000 per year,-at least, that was what it cost in 1932. speechtext:
It seems to me there is a
very important principle involved in the buying of stations. The right hon. gentleman a moment ago said that the price was fixed at $70,000 by the radio committee last session. I happen to have been a member of that committee and I am sure that the committee itself set' no values on any stations whatever. Possibly values were brought in by the engineer's of the radio branch of the Department of Marine. The point I desire to make is this. I have no fault to find if the government allows nothing for goodwill; in fact, I think there is an element of danger in the future acquisition of radio stations, and I believe it was pretty definitely brought out and established in the proceedings of the radio committee last year that no amount should be allowed for goodwill for the very good reason that all radio stations were operated under licence, and the licence

Radio-Purchase of C.NR. Stations
expired in all eases within the year, so that no goodwill was established. It was pretty definitely laid down and perhaps was recognized that in the purchase of these stations no private owners of radio stations should expect to be paid for goodwill, no matter how profitable their stations may have been. I think that the government in future purchases of radio stations should definitely and absolutely bear in mind that when they buy stations they should pay nothing for goodwill, because that was the understanding in the radio committee last year, and it is important.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: APPROVAL OF PURCHASE OF CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS BROADCASTING STATIONS
speechtext:
I think there is a great
principle involved in this matter. When the Canadian National Railways a few years ago embarked on the policy of radio broadcasting this policy was criticized a good deal by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were on this side of the house. At that time they said it was not right, that it was going to cost a lot of money. To-day we find that these same hon. gentlemen now that they are in office are trying to go out of the venture and to turn it over to the radio commission. As pointed out by my hon. friend from Quebec East, the advantage that is to be derived from the radio will all accrue to the Canadian Pacific Railway. That company will have the advantage of the operation of stations which they built and which they will continue to run in the future. By means of this legislation the administration is putting the Canadian National Railways in a most disadvantageous position as compared to the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian Pacific will have an advantage over the Canadian National. It is by such tactics that the government is curtailing the activities of the Canadian National Railways. I think this resolution should be considered most carefully as it seems to me to be a step in the wrong direction and one which will enure to the benefit of a competitor of the Canadian National Railways.
While I am On my feet I should like to ask the leader of the government if it is the intention of the government to take similar action in connection with stations operated by private individuals and companies. I refer particularly to the station operated by La Presse, to station CFCF and to the station recently licensed and operated by La Patrie. Is it the intention of the government to take over these stations and, if so, what basis of valuation will be used?

My hon. friends are asking if this is to be the basis upon which purchases will be made in the future. Then it will be the duty of the arbitrators to determine, according to the statute, the basis of the price and to decide whether an allowance for good-will will be made or not. I hold that this particular purchase is in the interests of the radio commission and of the Canadian National Railways. He is one of seventeen members on the board. My hon. friend, on one of his periodical visits from Montreal, now claims that the deputy minister was on the 
board. Certainly he was on the board. The deputy minister was on the board in 1929 when my hon. friends in the late government permitted the Canadian National to commit the country to $250,000,000 worth of expenditure. If that government was willing to take all that responsibility, probably we shall have to take it for this. But the deputy minister was not instructed by this government. Let me read the first fewT paragraphs of a statement which was handed to me by the Canadian National Railways and which is as much as I and this government know about the matter; except that we have to approve it just as parliament has to do. This is a statement dated February 10:
The board of directors decided in October, 3932, that we should take prompt steps to dispose of our radio broadcasting station and studio facilities and considered it desirable that the Canadian radio commission should be invited to acquire the Canadian National Railways station and studio facilities on a basis to be mutually agreed upon.
Negotiations were entered into with the radio commission through the director of publicity- that officer having taken charge of the radio activities of the Canadian National Railways in 1931.
The radio broadcasting commission has now made an offer of $50,000 for our facilities and also expresses its willingness, if its offer is accepted, to take over the personnel presently employed in the radio branch.
The transfer of the Canadian National Railways radio activities to the commission would effect a reduction in the railway's payroll of $45,000 per annum and a total reduction in expenses, founded upon 1932 experience, of upwards of $80,000 per annum.
The capital investment of the railway in the broadcasting facilities involved in the proposed transaction amounts to approximately $132,000 before depreciation charges. What the Minister of Railways pointed out with regard to the cost to the Canadian National Railways of radio broadcasting is quite correct. It was an expensive service to administer. Anyone who holds that it was not a necessary service is quite justified in taking that position. But as to the losses, one must remember that the Canadian National Railways operated a radio broadcasting service without revenue. They did not operate as a commercial station. They gave radio service to passengers on their trains; which was the purpose for which their stations were established. Whether or not the service lost money has no bearing at all on the value of the broadcasting equipment. Other stations operating as commercial stations are making money and have spent large sums of money in building up their stations. Therefore the fact that it was a good thing for the Canadian National Railways to dispose of the radio stations because they had no revenue from them should not in my opinion be the governing factor in deciding the value

of these stations. I consider that the value of a radio station should have some relation to the capital invested over a period of years. It should have some relation to the earning power of the station, some relation to depreciation and to replacement cost value.

The Minister of Marine, who has charge of the voting of the estimates of the radio commission, said to the house that in so far as the purchase of these stations is concerned no goodwill was considered; a satisfactory bargain was made because the owners of the stations thought it wise to get' rid of them. I do not think that should be the governing factor, because the minister then went on to say that he could not admit the suggestion of the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), that nothing should be allowed for goodwill because the licences lapse in a year. The minister denied that premise and said that in future he may allow for goodwill. Minister of Railways warmed up. But let us come back to cold facts. The Minister of Railways spoke about the expenditure on radio by the Canadian National Railways. In that respect Sir Henry Thornton was a pioneer. If it had not been for the radio policy of the Canadian National Railways we would have been without a station for many years. May I praise also the enterprise of the great Montreal paper La Presse, which has a very good station, CKAC. Now it is no longer the national railways who have to pay for that, it is the radio commission. In his wide experience as a lawyer can he give me any other instance where the purchaser fixes the price of the thing he wishes to buy, and the seller says nothing? The Canadian National Railways had only to accept a figure given by the radio commission, the Canadian National had the knife at their throat, if they had not accepted the government would have cut their throat. National Railways, and one for the radio commission. When the Canadian National Railways have a deficit they have to get the money from parliament to cover that deficit. speechtext:
I should like to congratulate my genial friend, the Minister of Railways, upon getting rid of a white elephant and receiving $50,000 for it. It -has been stated that the equipment of the Moncton station was second hand and the experience which we have had with it seems to bear out that statement.. At Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, there was a station with about one-
quarter the supposed power of the station at Moncton. We were able to hear that station quite distinctly while we never could get the Moncton station although we were only about 110 to 130 miles away. That station was of no value so far as the maritime provinces were concerned. Its value to-day is only as scrap. The steel towers whioh to-day are unsafe are worth just about the cost of taking them down. There is probably a certain amount of copper-covered wire which would be worth, say, a cent and a half per pound. I do not think the scrap value of the whole station will exceed $1,500 or $2,000. If the minister can unload these stations upon *some other department and receive $50,000 he is entitled to our congratulations. He is receiving mine, at least.

speechtext:

may be disputed by hon. members opposite, I contend that this is just another illustration of the way in which the Canadian National Railways was loaded up with extravagances. speechtext:

members have objections to other stations being taken over by the government at some distant time. I think the time to deal with that aspect of the question- will be when the government are in a position- to announce to the house that they intend to take over other stations. At the present time I do not intend to deal with that phase of the matter which seems to be somewhat extraneous to the question which we are now discussing. It has been claimed by some hon. members that we are not dealing fairly with the Canadian National railway system. Personally I feel that we are dealing fairly with the company. The price to -be paid -has been determined by the two parties to the transaction and evidently both are quite satisfied. The broadcasting system may have been a white elephant upon the hands of the railroad company but, on the other hand, it is quite obvious that this system may become a valuable asset to the radio commission. The railroad company was in the transportation business while the radio commission is in- the broadcasting business. The railway company did not have the advantage of the $2 fees which will be collected by the radio commission. These fees will pay the interest upon the capital invested,

and possibly pay off the capital itself. I feel that the radio commission is doing the obvious thing in taking over a utility which belonged to another department and I am satisfied that both sides have made a good bargain.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF PURCHASE OF CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS BROADCASTING STATIONS
speechtext:
I have no desire to delay the discussion but I would like to deal very briefly with two points which have been raised. The first is with regard to the policy of the government in the taking over of additional stations. It seems to me that this matter of policy was pretty well decided by the report of the radio committee which sat last session. I should like to read two of the clauses from the recommendations of that committee, as follows:
(a)	That one of the first duties of the commission be the establishment of trans-Canada chain broadcasting through the securing of the necessary land lines as soon as possible.
(b)	That a nationally-owned system of radio broadcasting be instituted, and that all stations required for its proper organization be eventually acquired, same to be financed from the revenues accruing to the business of broadcasting, without expense to the taxpayers through the public treasury.
I need not read any more than that. It seems to me that those recommendations lay down a pretty definite general policy in connection with broadcasting. I take it that the taking over of the Canadian National broadcasting system is the first step in the carrying out of that policy. I am not sure whether it is fair to expect the government to say at the moment just how fast they will move in carrying out the recommendations of the committee. It seems to me that the radio bill which was passed last session was passed for the distinct purpose of implementing the recommendations of the committee. It must be remembered that the report of the committee was adopted by the house. I am not going to find any particular fault-I certainly am not playing politics-if the government are not in a position to say that next year or the year after they will take over such and such a station. I take it that sooner or later

it ought to be sooner.-they will take possession of the general broadcasting business in Canada.

been granted. I have one particular station in mind and the proceedings in connection therewith certainly do not meet with my approval. There is one other point I would like to make. With all due deference to my good friend the Minister of Railways, I do not think he is quite fair in his reference to the outlays made by the Canadian National Railways in connection with broadcasting. After all, the purpose of the installation of receiving sets in the trains was not just an extravagant method of entertaining the passengers, it was a definite means of attracting business-just another form of advertising. I am not going to say just what success that advertising had-I might not have done the same thing if I bad been in authority-but I think it is true that the railway company did obtain considerable publicity through the installation of receiving sets on the trains. No one can say definitely what returns will be received from any particular form of advertising. The railways have expended hundreds of thousands and perhaps millions of dollars in advertising.

fere with the work of the commission, it is feebleness, it is weakness, it is unworthy of any minister of the crown. Who

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Many representations were made to us from different quarters in favour of the action which we have taken to admit Palestine oranges free of duty during the months indicated. This is an orange of superior quality and flavour and a certain amount of trade has developed with Palestine. We thought it was a move in the right direction.
Will this conflict with importations from other parts of the British Empire such as South Africa? Have there been any protests?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The only protest we have received from any part of the empire was from Jamaica. Palestine is a mandated territory, class A mandate, and even though we have oranges free under the British preference and subject to a duty of 35 cents per cubic foot

under the intermediate and general, last year we imported eighty-eight per cent of our oranges from the United States. There is therefore still ample room for the West Indian and more particularly the Jamaican orange. In these circumstances we felt that they had no legitimate right to complain of the free entry accorded to Palestine.

Will not this interfere with
the Australian treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, nor with South Africa; they ship in another season entirely. It does not interfere with them in the slightest degree.
These oranges are admitted in January, February, March and April; why not throughout the year? I understand they are very good oranges.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These months suit importation from Palestine. They are the only free months having regard to our treaties with South Africa and Australia.

These oranges are imported
into the old country months ahead of that. Why should they not come here in the month of December just as the Japanese oranges called tangerines do?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We could not grant free
entry in December because that month is preempted by the Australian treaty.

The only months during
which it is convenient for the people of Palestine to export are the months mentioned.

Was there a delegation
from the West Indies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A delegate came from the
island of Jamaica and had an interview with the government, and while I cannot say that he went away satisfied, we were able to give him evidence to show that his people were more alarmed than hurt.

With respect to the protest made by Jamaica in this matter, it occurs to me that our obligation is greater to the West Indies than it is to Palestine, which is a mandated country. Of course, I am interested in Palestine and all its early associations, but commercially our obligations should be discharged first to the AVest Indies. Is there likely to be any conflict? I do not like the thought of Jamaica being jostled to one side.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend that, other things being equal, we should give the preference to those within the empire. Without any treaty obligations, and outside the West Indian treaty, we gave free entry to Jamaica the year round, and I pointed out to the delegate from that island that they were not presenting a good case to us when they indicated that their objection to free entry on the part of Palestine oranges was that Jamaica would have to come into competition with Palestine and that therefore their oranges w'ould sell at a lower price. I suggested to them that it was rather a peculiar representation to make to a minister of the Canadian government, that the Canadian people would secure oranges at a lower price. As a matter of fact however, on balance, I think Canada has dealt very fairly, if not indeed generously, with the West Indies. We give them the benefit of a splendid steamship service which costs this country around three quarters of a million a year, and in that connection I may point out, as I pointed out to the representative of Jamaica, that frequently if West Indian shippers have an opportunity to use a tramp steamer they do so to the detriment of the Canadian service which is put on at a great expense. Furthermore, through our preference to West Indian sugar, which the West Indian avails himself of to the last fraction of a cent, we are in effect giving a subvention to the West Indies amounting to several millions a year. Then, bearing in mind the further fact that there is still an opportunity in the Canadian market to replace a portion of that eighty-eight per cent supplied last year by the United States, I think we have treated the Jamaicans fairly in the circumstances, if not generously.

So long as it is
understood that all mandated countries are to be considered as being on a parity with our British dominions and colonies, and if we are under an obligation in that respect, I have nothing further to say. I do not think however that we should go out of our way to put such countries on an equal footing with other parts of the empire if they are not actually so. The fact that Jamaica may not happen to have a good case is merely incidental; another colony might have an excellent case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

agricultural machinery. It has been discussed in the house on different occasions, it was brought up last session and again this session. It contains one very interesting stipulation:
Complete parts for repairs, under regulations prescribed by the minister.
I have no doubt the house would like to have an assurance that these regulations will not be of the kind passed last year, about May 25, when a distinction was drawn between repair parts imported by the makers of implements and those that were imported by other persons, notably the companies in Winnipeg that undertook to import parts from the United States from those concerns that make repair parts for all implements. This was proved to be a very serious matter last year. It meant that the price of these parts was increased to the consumer here during the season. I am told that in some districts in Saskatchewan dealers failed to provide themselves with repair parts and farmers were put to great inconvenience. The regulation passed last year was one of the most iniquitous I have known. It made a distinction between two classes of dealers in the same goods. We are happy to know that the protests made against this regulation were effective. This item contains the words, "under regulations prescribed by the minister," and I would like to get the assurance of the minister that no regulation similar to the one passed last year will be introduced in connection with this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The purpose of this item is to eliminate the provision which was included in the item some three years ago limiting its operation to a period of time. The time for the application of this item was extended upon two different occasions and if the present item was not included it would mean that higher rates of duty would have prevailed after March of this year. Our intention is to make permanent the present existing low rates. In reply to the hon. member for Lisgar may I say that the words, "under regulations prescribed by the minister" appear in innumerable items in the tariff. These words have appeared in this .particular item for a number of years and they were in the item during the administration of the government which I assume my hon. friend supported upon occasions.
They did not pass the regulations which this government did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I could not give any undertaking as to what regulations will be prescribed by the present or any future Minister

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
of Finance. However, I can assure my hon. friend that there is nothing sinister in the item and I have no doubt it will be administered to his satisfaction.
After the trouble the government got into last year, I am sure they will not repeat their action.

I have not as much confidence in the government as has the hon. member for Lisgar. The Minister of National Revenue can do anything he likes as far as the tariff is concerned and there is no finality in any of the regulations which may be passed by the government. During the past few years the farmers have been buying very few new implements; they are tinkering and patching up the old machinery. It was little short of a crime to shoot up the tariff on repair parts the way it was done last year. Even after the rates were reduced, they were still ridiculously high. Some of the dealers in the smaller villages were unable to carry stocks and any repair parts ordered had to be sent from Regina or Winnipeg. They were sent by express and with the express charges added to the duty it made the cost of the repairs almost prohibitive. In some cases it would have been almost cheaper to buy a new machine. I warn the government that if there is any more of that kind of monkeying there will be a row all over Canada. If that kind of thing is repeated the government will need to tie their heads on their shoulders if they do not want something to happen.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: In view of what has been said, I feel I should say a word or two in answer. The speaker who first introduced this subject seems to be treating matters regardless of the facts. I am surprised that a gentleman with his past history and the knowledge which we know he possesses should make statements which are wholly untrue. There was no regulation passed that had a different application to one from that which it had to another, and I defy my hon. friend to produce such a regulation. In reply to the former Minister of Agriculture I would say that his friends out there did not want to buy anything else but goods made in the United States.
That is all nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
One firm wrote to me
and told me that they had sent out 1,800 circulars. What did those circulars say? They stated that because of the action taken by the government they had been compelled to increase their prices ten per cent and knock off the cash discount which had previously been
given. That was an erroneous statement. What happened? As soon as this action was finally taken an hon. member of this house asked the government to refund the money which had been paid in duty. After they had said that they had taken care of this matter in the manner I have indicated, the plea was put forward by an hon. member that the government should return the money which had been paid in duty.

I had nothing to do with the action taken by any of these companies. I have not the slightest doubt that commercial companies would take such action as that indicated by the Minister of National Revenue. The minister has stated that I made a statement which was not in accordance with the facts. I want to know what that statement was. We will have to go into this matter a little more fully. We are all aware of the course which was pursued with regard to the duties on repair parts for agricultural implements. We know that the application of the higher rates of duty was postponed from time to time. About March 1, or some time early last session, the hon. member for South Battle-ford brought this matter to the attention of the Prime Minister. At that time the Prime Minister gave a somewhat discourteous answer. He intimated that the hon. member should know better than to ask a question which could be answered only after the budget had been brought down.
Is that discourteous?
It is typical.

The higher rates of duty
were to be imposed on April 1 and about that date the hon. member for South Battleford asked the Minister of Finance for information regarding the higher rates of duties. The Minister of Finance stated that he was happy to inform the hon. member that the matter was being taken care of by order in council. A few days later the budget came down and the Minister of Finance stated that there was only one change in the tariff. He referred to this particular item and indicated that the lower rates of duty would be in effect for another year. We accepted that as satisfactory. But some time about May 25, so we are informed, while this house was still in session, an order went forth from some department of government, either finance or inland revenue, that those lower rates of duties should apply only when repairs were imported from firms that actually made the implements and the higher rates of duty were imposed upon all repair
4274	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
parts produced by companies across the line which make a specialty of manufacturing repair parts.
I had occasion to buy some ploughshares. They are perhaps one of the most important items that come into this particular list. When these companies began to supply the farmers with ploughshares, we were able to get for about $5 ploughshares for which we formerly paid $10 a pair. The dealer in my town, who, I believe, is a supporter of this government-and I do not know whether he will be at the next election; I do not think he will-along with other dealers brought the matter to my attention and the fact was that the price of ploughshares was raised, I cannot at the moment say how much. What we object to-and the statement I have made is in accordance with the fact-is that the high rates of duty were imposed upon repair parts coming from the United States when they were imported from companies manufacturing repair parts, but they were not imposed when the repair parts were imported from companies that made the machines for which the repair parts were intended. If I have made any statement that is not in accordance with fact, I want the Minister of National Revenue to tell me what that statement is. I have stated the case exactly as it exists.
The matter was brought to my attention by a Winnipeg film the head of which, I may say, has also been a supporter of this government. I have known him for many years as a Conservative. As soon as I got his letter, I wrote to the minister about it. I did not receive a reply for some time, but later I got an answer stating that the government was considering the question. Before I came to the house last fall, I went to the head of the firm in Winnipeg and asked whether the matter was exactly as he had represented it to me in the early part of the summer. I found that no change had been made; that the high rates of duty were still being imposed and collected. On the first opportunity I had I presented the matter to the house and we had the satisfaction of knowing that two days afterward the obnoxious regulation was cancelled. These are the facts of the case. My object in speaking of it now is just to ensure that such a regulation will not be passed again, and that no distinction will be made between two makers of ploughshares or anything else. Have I made any statement that is not in accordance with facts?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: If the hon. member will sit down, I will tell him.
The minister took occasion to make a somewhat sneering remark that from what he knew of me he would not have thought I would make such a statement. That was altogether uncalled' for.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The statement to which I referred is, I have no doubt, within the recollection of the house, and if not, it will be found in Hansard to-morrow. He said that regulations were made by the administration which had different applications to different people, and some were privileged and some were not. I say that that is not correct.

If I heard the minister aright, he has not made an explanation at all, and he certainly made a gross misstatement a little while ago when he said that I and my friends insisted on buying our repairs from the United States. That is a contemptible libel. I wish I had stronger language to use and could get past the chairman with it; and I want it to be considered as having been used. The farmers of the west, prior to this government coming into power, were more and more buying agricultural machinery in Canada. There was such a low tariff we could afford to do this and good feeling had developed between the farmers of the west and the farm implement manufacturers who were doing well, under a low duty. This tribe across the floor, after raising the duty on implements all along the line to 25 per cent and promising to keep the duty on repairs down to the old Liberal duty as if that were a great act of grace and compassion to the farmers, did not even keep that promise. They put the duty on repair parts up to the same rate as that on the original machinery. Then the Minister of National Revenue, after his own colleagues had apparently disciplined him into reducing the duty by a change in regulations tells us that we are making untruthful statements when, as a matter of fact, if he would examine himself he would not have to go out of his own seat to find that it was he who was making untruthful statements. I do not know what else to do except to go across the floor and see what I can do further by way of persuasion, with my hon. friend. Those of us who have had to lose our hides in buying farm machinery repairs know the difference between 25 per cent and 15 per cent, and we know the difference between six per cent and 25 per cent on the original article; yet they try to mislead the people outside and my friends to my left will tell us that there is no difference between the two parties with respect to the tariff. One is just four times as high as the

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
other on nearly all the farm machinery we use. We thought we were getting a little mite of a concession that one might put in one's eye and see none the worse for it, with regard to repairs; then the government took that away and tried to flim-flam the people that they did not do such a thing. It was his own colleagues plus himself, since the house met last October, that passed the regulation to lower the duty on repairs and thus remove the grievance complained of. The farmers of the west, in these times of depression, do not care where the repair parts are made; very few know where they are made; all they know is that this government socks them every time with high duties and hard regulations difficult to comply with.
Did the minister tell the hon. member for Lisgar wherein he made a misstatement? No; he gives us just the usual mumbling reply, trying to get past, but, if I know anything about the matter, he is not going to get past this time.

Not a member from Manitoba on that side will say that I have not stated the facts, because they have had representations from these machine companies just as I have, and I have no doubt they have made representations on the subject to the minister. I am not going to submit to the remark that I made a statement which was not in accordance with facts. I have stated the facts. Will the minister himself say that the duty on repair parts coming from the United States was not 25 per cent? No; he will not make the statement. Well, that is all the statement I made and the distinction was between the two classes of dealers I have indicated.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The statement I made was explicit; it was in answer to the hon. member for Lisgar's remark that regulations with a different application to different companies had been made by the Minister of National Revenue. That is contrary to the fact.
What is the fact?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Anything that was done by the Minister of National Revenue had application to everybody who came under any such regulation. If Hansard is consulted tomorrow, it will be found that the hon. member for Lisgar made the statement I have said he did.
With regard to the ex-Minister of Agriculture, I must say that he certainly gets away with a great deal, but it is a pleasure to listen to him. He occupies a unique position in the house. He can make any statement, and eome-53719-270
times those of us who cannot possibly agree with any part of what he is saying are pleased indeed to hear him carry on something that is in the nature of, well, I will not say buffoonery, but if anyone else can think of some word that is parliamentary to describe it, I will endorse it. The point is clear that those who are interested in this matter wanted to get their parts from the United States. The fact that the item is in the tariff shows that. The hon. ex-Minister of Agriculture denies that, although the item could have no application to anything else.
You could not get them anywhere else. They are manufactured only in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Of course, but the exMinister of Agriculture does not take that into consideration at all. He gives us a pleasant harangue which we can enjoy because there is humour in it if there is not sense.
We cannot say the same of yours.

Let us take a concrete case. I have a John Deere plough. I could buy shares from the United States made by this company which makes a specialty of manufacturing parts for $5 a pair; I am giving approximate figures. If I buy John Deere shares in Canada from a John Deere company I pay about $10 a pair. That is the situation that we objected to. The 25 per cent duty was levied against this cheaper class of shares which we have found in our experience serve our purpose just as well as the higher priced shares. The same is true of binder canvas and a number of other items, but ploughshares are the biggest item in the list. The minister may quibble about the duty being applied to all people. Well, I suppose that is true of all people importing exactly the same kind of goods. But here we have two classes of importers or dealers who are handling repair parts and in each case the parts serve the purpose for which they were intended, but in one case a duty of 25 per cent is applied and in the other a duty of 6 iper cent. So the Minister of National Revenue cannot get away with any quibbling of that kind.
I took up with the Minister of National Revenue the matter which the hon. member for Lisgar has mentioned long before he had anything to do with it.
You did not get any results.

I did. You see the results to-day. I know to whom my hon. friend is referring. It is Mr. Ackland. The hon. member for Lisgar is trying to take all the credit.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
As a matter of fact the farmers of the west are buying agricultural machinery cheaper today by 25 per cent than they could buy it under hon. gentlemen opposite. What more evidence do you want? By the way, when the hon. member for Lisgar talks about "shears" does he mean ploughshares? Shares is the right pronunciation, and I am glad to put him right. If he does not understand it, let him look it up in the dictionary. The gentleman to whom my hon. friend referred was a Conservative and he came to me in the Carlton Club and told me that a certain firm was manufacturing these parts in the United States, and that they could be supplied in this country. I brought the matter, as I have said, to the attention of the minister and he was kind enough to remedy the situation, and now my hon. friend from Lisgar is trying to take the credit for it. He wants to go back to Lisgar and parade as a low tariff champion, that he has done something for agricultural implements. Why, Mr. Chairman, forty years ago when the duty was 35 per cent I bought a binder for $120 or $130, as did many hon. gentlemen and they were cheaper then even with that duty than you can buy them to-day. What does it matter what the duty is as long as you can buy the implements cheaper? I repeat, you can buy them cheaper to-day than you could under hon. gentlemen opposite.

The minister must be praying to be saved from his friends. The hon. member for Marquette said that he went to the minister with a grievance and that the minister remedied it. What was the grievance and what was the remedy? That is what we want to know. As a matter of fact, the remedy came two days after I brought the matter to the attention of the house last fall.

The hon. gentleman has asked me a question and I want to answer it. The remedy was that Mr. Ackland came to see me, and I think my hon. friend from Lisgar will agree that he came to me before he came to him. I brought the matter to the attention of the minister and that situation was remedied, and to-day you can buy ploughshares cheaper than you could years ago when my hon. friends opposite were in power.

There is no question
that the facts were as stated. Repair parts were to come in under a low rate of duty, 6, 7 and 10 per cent. Unquestionably the duty was so arranged by regulation that the low rates applied to the manufacturers of certain lines of goods, but certain dealers termed pirate dealers had to pay the higher rate of duty, 25 per cent, on ploughshares, [Mr. Mullins.1
binder canvas and other articles. There is no doubt at all that that increased the price. Complaints were made by many farmers from western Canada that the price had been increased by at least the difference in the duty. Naturally the matter was brought to the attention of the government and finally it was rectified. As to who deserves the credit I do not know or care. A great many members from the west, Conservative, Liberal and Progressive, were all familiar with the*?aets. I was one of those who sent a wire to the Prime Minister, and others did, and perhaps action was brought about as the cumulative effect of pressure from all sides and by the irrefutable facts themselves. The facts were as has been stated. The situation was brought about by a regulation, and the result was a higher price, and every farmer in Canada knew it.

I think it has been amply confirmed that there was a grievance, and so far as I am concerned, I am willing that the hon. member for Marquette Should get the credit for redressing that grievance by going to somebody and he going to somebody else, and finally to the government. The reason we are bringing this question up to-night is that we want no more monkey-shining of that nature, either with repairs or anything else. What happened was that after we got a statement in the house assuring us that we would get a low rate on repairs, after we went home a higher rate was applied. We do not want to have that kind of business repeated. Apparently the Minister of National Revenue thought that what I was saying a few minutes ago was an attempt at humour. I never felt less like being humorous in my life. Apparently my 'hon. friend does not appreciate when I feel like going to the ex-tremest lengths possible in trying to get a little horse sense filtered through his cranium on agricultural matters. I 'hope the Minister of Finance will take his colleagues in charge and if the government are going to let him run at large much longer, at least let them give him the hint that he must not repeat his unwarranted action of last year.

There is no doubt whatever that there was a grievance in regard to the importation of repair parts for agricultural implements. The hon. member for Marquette has admitted that there was one, and we all know it. With regard to the manufacture of implements, there are two classes of cases. We have in western Canada farmers who came in there from the United States, good farmers, and who brought their machinery with them-

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
not that they wanted to buy machinery made in the United States rather than that made in Canada, but they had this machinery and brought it with them. There are hundreds of them in my constituency. Many of these old implement concerns in the United States have gone out of business, and therefore owners of the machinery are not able to get repairs from the parent company. But many companies have started up all through the United States making repair parts for different machines. These men could not get repair parts from these manufacturers in the United States without paying the higher rate of duty. If you had a John Deere plough, as the hon. member (for Lisgar mentioned, you could order a ploughshare from the John Deere company in the United Staes and get it in at the lower rate of duty, but if you ordered it from one of these repair part concerns you had to pay the higher rate. That was the grievance, because hundreds of people could not order from the parent company; there was no parent company and they were obliged to order from these repair part companies. Therefore, as the hon. member for Lisgar said, the regulations did not apply equally, one man paid a low rate of duty and another had to pay a high rate. So when the hon. member for Lisgar said that regulations were passed by this government that did not apply to all people alike, he said what was absolutely true. That is what Mr. Ackland referred to. He handles these repair parts, not for any line company but for the different agencies in the United States, and he was anxious to get this lower rate of duty so that he could sell on the same low cost as before. What we are asking for to-night is that the minister will see that no such regulation is made effective again, whereby some have to pay a high rate of duty and others a low rate. This regulation continued in force all last summer; the grievance was not remedied until the fall when repair parts were not needed. It is in the summer time we do the farming, not in the winter.

The Minister of National Revenue made a statement that we on this side of the house cannot allow to go unchallenged. He stated that our friends in the west wanted to make all their purchases in the United States. The effect of the regulation that he put into force last year was not to stop the importation of goods from the United States, but to say to the farmers of the west: If you want to buy goods imported from the United States you must buy them from certain favoured individuals. A certain charmed circle were given the benefit of the 53719-270J
lower rate; everyone outside that circle was compelled to pay the higher rate. Those belonging to the charmed circle were charging a price nearly twice as great as the others were charging. The minister had no right to make the statement he did, and we resent it. We resent the attempt to force our purchases into the hands of particular manufacturers.

The hon. gentleman is wrong. Manufacturers of agricultural implements in the United States can always bring in their repair parts at the lower rate. These ploughshares imparted by Mr. Ackland were sold by the blacksmiths throughout the country and sold cheaper. I do not want the hon. member to take all the credit for that, because I think I had something to do with it, in fact I think the Minister of National Revenue will bear me out when I say that I had considerable to do with it. However, if it is any satisfaction for the member for Lisgar to take the credit and to get a few.-votes, it does not bother me.
Why didn't you start earlier?

May I ask the hon'.
member for Marquette one question? Why didn't the hon. member have the minister rectify it before the winter if he was so much interested in the farmers getting cheaper implements? The hon. member for Marquette knows that if you buy repair parts from these independent companies you can buy them at least seventy-five per cent cheaper than you could from the companies which make the machines. The farmer was buying these parts from independent companies who do nothing else but make repair parts, for the simple reason that he could not afford to pay the prices the parent companies were charging. Yet this government and the Minister of National Revenue put a duty of twenty-five per cent on those cheap repairs, which the farmer needs to-day more than ever because the prices of his commodities have gone away down, and allowed repairs to come in from the parent companies at six per cent duty. Yet my hon. friend from Marquette, who wants to take credit for having this duty removed, allowed it to go on all summer. If my hon. friend from Marquette has as much influence with the minister as he claims, he should have used it throughout the summer and not allowed this injustice to continue for six or seven months.

The hon. gentleman is
entirely wrong. I brought it to the attention of the minister and it did not take all summer. It has been remedied. I want to ask

these two hon. gentlemen who arc championing cheap implements if they a^e not now buying implements ten or twenty per cent, yes thirty per oent cheaper than they were before?
I will answer the question if you will let me.

This talk about the tariff bogy is all for votes; there is nothing to it. We are buying implements cheaper to-day than we ever did under the regime of the hon. gentlemen, any time from 1822 to 1930.
Mr. . BEAUBIEN:	Since this government
has been in power the farmer has no purchasing power to buy implements, and he has to buy repairs.

Where? Canada or
the United States?
Where they make them.
I realize it just as well as hon. gentlemen opposite.
Then you should not be sitting over there.

You are just playing to

I don't care two Straws about getting on Hansard, but I want to play fair. .1 am as much a champion of cheaper implements and of aid to the farmer in western *Canada as either of the hon. gentlemen opposite who spoke.

The hon. member for
Marquette knows that the duty on these implements was equalized in the month of October, doesn't he?
The hon. gentleman knows very well it has been remedied, does he not? Will he answer the question, yes or no?
Yes, it has been remedied.

Then whait more do you

I can say to the Minister of National Revenue and to the hon. member for Marquette, that it was rectified in October, but the duty was imposed all summer, when we needed repairs. I am pleading with the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Revenue and the hon. member for Marquette not to allow the same trick to be played this summer. That is the point. I hope my hon. friend from Marquette will see the Minister of

National Revenue before he goes back to his constituency, or see him now, and tell him that if he ever does that sort of thing again he will cross the floor and join the C.C.F.

The hon. member has
taken too much on himself. I want to ask what he was doing during the eight years his party was in power. To-day in western Canada we have cheaper machinery than we have had for several years

I should like to make an
explanation, in case any person might accuse me of making a wrong statement. I want it to be understood that the ploughshares to which I referred are not the same type of shares mentioned by my hon. friend. One is called the soft centre share, and this is supposed to be the best ploughshare, but the farmers have found from actual experience that the crucible share, which is imported from the United States, serves their purpose equally well. That is the share to which I referred, and I want that understood in case it might be thought that I was referring to the same implement.

After this extended controversy with regard to repairs to farm implements, Mr. Chairman, in view of the unemployment problem in Canada I should like to ask the minister if some means could not be devised whereby all this repairing could be done in Canada by Canadians.

After consultation with the British authorities, they agreed to a restoration of the duty to 10 per cent instead of the 15 per cent which had hitherto obtained under the British preference.

The minister says that under the present tariff the British preferential rate on electric telephone apparatus and complete parts thereof was free, but under the proposed tariff there is a duty of 10 per cent. That means an increase of 10 per cent. He says that this has been arrived at by conference with the British government in order to save an industry in Canada. speechtext: Yes.

Does he know the Northern
Electric Company is a subsidiary of the Bell Telephone Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no official knowledge of that fact; in fact I do not know I have any private knowledge; it may be so.

I am going to object to this
increase in tariff, because it affects telephone companies in other parts of Canada. If this item goes through, the maritime telephone companies, for instance, the Nova Scotia Telephone Company and the New Brunswick Telephone Company and, I presume, the telephone companies of the west, will have to pay tribute to the Northern Electric Company. It is a well known fact that the Northern Electric Company is a subsidiary of the Bell Tele-

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
phone Company; that the Bell Telephone owns 51 per cent of the Northern Electric and that the balance of the stock is owned by another manufacturer of the same kind of goods in the United States. It is not fair to other telephone companies that instead of their being able to import these goods from Great Britain at a 10 per cent reduction, this special duty of 10 per cent is imposed in order to keep the British goods out or to compel the other telephone companies to pay an additional 10 per cent on their equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the first place my hon.
friend for years supported a government which imposed a duty of 15 per cent under the British preference on these articles and they were placed upon the free list by this government as a result of the conference agreements. But it has been found out that, having regard to the difference between the wage paid to British and that paid to Canadian artisans, this industry could not live under free competition. The question is not one of the Bell Telephone Company or the Northern Electric Company as being its subsidiary, if it is; that is not important. The question is this: That industry under normal conditions employes 7,000 workmen and pays out in wages $10,000,000 a year. It would be a very serious matter to the industrial life of Canada and to the city of Montreal in particular if that industry were wiped out as it would be if the item remained free under the British preference. I think the circumstance that the British government have assented to our representations in this respect is evidence of the reasonableness of the request made to them to vary the conference agreement in this one regard only.
Some hon. gentlemen opposite-and I do not object to this-have seized upon certain articles where an increase in duty is imposed, but they allow to pass, without a word emanating from them, item after item which have been carried this afternoon and evening either placing articles on a lower scale of duty or making them free.
Of course.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Of the fifty-seven articles
in the budget, to say nothing of the amendments which I have submitted to-night, all of Which are for a lowering of duty, only five refer to an increase 'in the tariff and the remainder refer to either a lowering of tariff or a widening of the item. I think it is important that these considerations should be borne in mind.
Is my hon. friend objecting to our not criticising the reductions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not at all, but I am just
drawing attention to the emphasis in the one case as contrasted with the silence in the other.
When the minister does well, we approve.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Not openly.

I do not think the first part of the minister's reply to what I said was a real answer. For instance, he referred to the fact that I had supported a government which had imposed a duty of fifteen per cent on these articles. Let me say-
Carried.

If my hon. friend is in favour of the Bell Telephone Company or the Northern Electric Company, all right; I am not. It is quite true that I supported that government, but the Minister of Finance knows I am not in favour of any tariff, whether fifteen per cent or ten per cent, or five per cent. I am a free trader; I believe there should be no tariff restrictions, because the manufacturer in every case takes advantage of those tariffs and the consumer has to suffer. Whether it be the Northern Electric or any other company, if they cannot produce in this country goods as cheaply as we can buy them in Great Britain, then they should not be protected. We have heard a great deal in other days about flapping the flag, the mother country, and all the rest of it. Here we have the telephone companies, which are really the consumers of this commodity, not 'being able to buy from Great Britain because the government imposes a duty of ten per cent. I cannot agree with the minister's, shall I call it sob story, when he says that if this duty is not imposed, a certain number of men will be put out of work. I should like to know how much money the Northern Electric Company made in the last ten or twelve years. I should like to see a financial statement in order to find out whether this ten per cent duty is necessary. I say it is not; these people can manufacture the goods cheaply 'and they do not require the duty. It is not in the interests of the people of Canada that other telephone companies, owing to the imposition of this ten per cent duty, are taken by the throat and compelled to buy these goods from the Northern Electric instead of being able to buy them in the open market where they can get them the cheapest. If there were four or five companies in this country manufacturing these articles, the matter might be different.

to task for objecting to this raising of duty. He says that in the whole budget there are only some five or six items on which the duties are raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I may say to my hon. friend that I did not take him nor any of his associates to task; that is one of the last things I would wish to do. But it is the right and the privilege of every hon. member to express his views; my hon. friend will not, I hope, deny that right to me, and he must not object if my view does not exactly coincide with his. My hon. friend will not think, I am sure, that I am taking him or anyone else to task if I venture to disagree with what he or his associates may say. My hon. friend made the bald statement that the majority of the tariff amendments lowering the duty had been made in favour of the manufacturer. As a matter of fact in a moment or two I shall be able to give my hon. friend the exact proportion. I can say now that the majority of the reductions were not in favour of the manufacturer either in number, volume or importance, but that on the contrary the majority in number, in volume, in importance, and in value are in favour of individuals as against the manufacturer.
If the minister thinks we have been negligent in expressing our appreciation-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not complaining.

-I hasten to correct that omission on our part. I am not very much concerned whether the duties were lowered for the benefit of the manufacturer or of the individual. In so far as they have been lowered they meet with my approval. In regard to this particular item it is rather an unfortunate time to increase the duty on telephone supplies when so many thousands of people in the western provinces are taking out their telephones. Indeed, the taking out of the telephones is one source of embarrassment to the provincial governments in the west at the present time. They constructed these telephone lines on borrowed money, and it looked like good business and it was good business. The revenue was paying all the expenses, but now the telephones are being removed by the thousands, and the consequence will be that the provinces will suffer in their finances at a very unfortunate time. There is another thing which might have been taken into account and that is that this question might have been submitted to the tariff board before the duty was reimposed. The tariff board will have to consider this question of the relative cost of manufacture in England and in Canada, and it might very properly have been submitted to the tariff board which has now been constituted, before any action was taken. It just goes to show that from the standpoint of the consumer and of those who believe in the entry of goods under lower tariffs the British agreement is just that much worse than we thought it was last fall, by the removal of these items from a tariff which did seem to offer some relief to the consumer.

speechtext: This is designed to modernize the item. Hitherto certain plates could be imported free of duty for the purpose of enabling magazines to be printed in Canada, and the effect has been to give employment to a large amount of labour in printing magazines, several score in number, which prior to the tariff item of two years ago were printed in the United States and imported duty free. The photograph has the effect, as I understand it, of etching the cylinder and producing a class of work which cannot be distinguished from set type. This polygraphic process will now be permitted free entry for the purpose of allowing the printing of magazines in Canada precisely as was hitherto the case with the plates.

That may be the opinion of the government, but it is not the opinion

of the printers, the practical men engaged in the trade. This is a copy of a letter or resolution sent to the Prime Minister from Toronto Typographical Union No. 91. Towards the end of the resolution it says:
With hundreds of our typesetters out of work, we are amazed to find that it is proposed to allow plates to enter Canada duty free, thus taking away the only chance to place these men hack at work.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I gay to my hon. friend that this very item is designed to give employment to Canadian labour. If it does not go through there will be less Canadian labour employed. Hitherto plates have come in, stereotypes and electrotypes-
Mats.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, giving a -replica of the magazine as published in the United States. It has been the means of giving largely increased employment to labour in Canada. Permitting the polygraph process to come in the same as the plates have hitherto done is merely modernizing the item, not changing the original intent at all.

Mr. Chairman, I hold in my hand a brief submitted by the Toronto typographical union. I am fully conversant with the fact that the mats were imported into Canada, that the typesetting was done in the United States. I am conversant with the legislation that is in force in that country which prevents the importation of those mats into that country. In this brief, of which I think the minister has a copy, the typographical union complain of that condition in Canada. It hardly seems possible to me-
I am not a practical printer, I am merely passing on information that is sent to me- that the men engaged in the industry should be fearful of the conditions that would be brought about by the granting of their request.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend overlooks one fact, and so do those for whom he speaks, who would agree with him, and that is that prior to 1931 when we placed a duty on American magazines, the whole magazine, all the labour, all the paper, ink and expenditure which went into its make-up, came from the United States. But after we imposed the duty it was found to be to the advantage of the American publishers to come over into Canada, which they did in large numbers. To-day scores of American magazines are being printed in Canada, providing labour for scores of Canadians, using Canadian paper and ink, and this is in part by reason of the fact that they are able to bring in the plates from the United States. And the negative is the modern process; it merely permits a continuation of a system which I submit has been to the advantage of the Canadian people as a whole and of Canadian labour in particular.

Mr. Chairman, everything the minister says is true. The type of publication involved is such as True Stories- you know the kind of magazine I mean. The amount of actual labour has not been greatly increased, the cost of publication has been lessened. The circulation has been increased; predictions made at that time that it would reduce the circulation of this kind of publication have not been fulfilled. What the typesetters object to is the importation of these mats. They feel that they should receive the same protection that the printers in the United States receive. The law there definitely states that for anything that is printed in that country the type shall be set up in the United States. I would rather take the advice of a man engaged in the printing trades than my own opinion or that of a member of this house. They feel that this is going to throw hundreds of their men out of work and possibly deny them employment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: If the placing of a duty on these plates would reduce the circulation of such magazines as True Stories, Film Fun and Ballyhoo, probably it would be better for the people of this country, particularly the younger .people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend must not allow it to appear that this printing is confined to Film Fun, Ballyhoo and magazines of that class, some of which are actually prohibited to-day.
They are on the news stands.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That may be so, but some of them will not be there to-morrow. I may tell my hon. friend that many high class magazines are being printed in Canada to-day as a result of the tariff imposed.

I am afraid this is another statement that will hardly bear investigation. Under the tariff policy of the government many of the better class magazines have had their circulation materially diminished. Only this week I saw a statement with regard to about a dozen of the better class magazines, including the Atlantic Monthly and Harper's Magazine, which showed that the circulation had been reduced by from 36 per cent to 40 per cent, while in the case of the Literary Digest I think the reduction was about 81 per cent. We recognize the fact that these higher class magazines are very desirable, but the net result of the tariff policy of this government in regard to magazines has been just as the minister has stated j they have permitted the importation of the plates of the trashy magazines, though I do not say they are all objectionable. In the main, however, they are the lower class of magazines and they have increased their circulation or, if not, certainly 
they have not lost circulation, while to a large extent the higher class magazines have been excluded.

For the sake of argument, however, let us admit that the policy of the government with respect to magazines is wrong. I see that the
regulations are to be prescribed by the minister, and presumably that is the Minister of National Revenue. I wonder if I could get the attention of the Minister of Finance for a moment to ask just how these regulations are prescribed and carried into effect. My understanding is that the minister, or some of his staff, prepares the regulations and brings them to council, and council accepts, amends or rejects them. Then they are gazetted, after which they become law. Is that the procedure, or are they ministerial orders, determined entirely by the Minister of National Revenue? Perhaps I could get the minister's attention for a moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is getting my attention; I was simply directing a question to my official in order to answer my hon. friend. I was listening to every word he said. This provision with regard to the regulations to be prescribed by the minister has been here for years; we are not just inserting that now. The effect of the item is to enlarge the free importation for hospital use by adding parts for hospital tables. In this way the duty on these parts is reduced from 35 per cent to free. With respect to the regulations, since this is a hospital item those regulations would have to do with the proper policing of the importations to see that they were put to hospital use only. The regulations would be prepared by the Department of National Revenue, and would not of necessity be subject to order in council. They might be discussed in council, but they would not be the subject of order in council. May I point out to my hon. friend, however, that heretofore any person aggrieved had the right to appeal to the board of customs, but since the tariff board act has been passed, after May 1 of this year an appeal would lie to the tariff board. So I am sure my hon. friend will be gratified to know that there is an additional safeguard so far as the activity of the Minister of National Revenue is concerned.

That is some safeguard, of course, but I was a little afraid that the recital would be just about what it was. As a rule regulations prescribed by the minister meant, ini my time at all events, that the regulations were submitted to council and there agreed to or amended as the circumstances warranted, after which they were gazetted. Now it appears that they are to be ministerial orders under certain circumstances, and the only remedy is an appeal to the tariff board. This looks worse than I
anticipated. It would appear, then, that almost all these items we are considering come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Revenue without the necessity of submitting the regulations to council at all. In other words, if be wants to do some more pegging of the pound or fixing of valuation for duty purposes or for dumping duty propositions, nine-tenths of it will be in the hands of the Minister of National Revenue no matter what this parliament decides. I wonder if there is not some way of getting a twitch on the Minister of National Revenue so that we may have some of the desires of this parliament carried into effect with regard to' tariffs. So far as I am concerned, I know that it was very rarely in the days of the Liberal government that a ministerial order had such wide significance as it has to-day. Possibly the same law existed but it was very seldom made use of it. But now, with the door open to the Minister of National Revenue, we are decidedly alarmed at his activities in managing by many devices to put up the tariff, while his colleagues may know nothing about it.
Mr. RHODES1:	My hon. friend is unduly
alarmed. I would remind him that he sat in the government for nine years while this same provision was in the tariff. He may be somewhat perturbed by my colleague the Minister of National Revenue, but I can assure him that he has no reason to be. I am sure the hon. gentleman will realize that there is no other method whereby the item could be administered. Let me give a concrete illustration. If a sterilizer were brought in for use in a laundry it would be subject to a duty of thirty-five per cent, whereas under this provision, if brought in for a hospital, it is duty free. When the tariff provides that regulations shall be prescribed by the Minister of National Revenue it simply means that when, for instance, a sterilizer is brought in for hospital purposes it shall be bona fide for such use and not brought in under that guise and then surreptitiously used in a laundry.

I am aware that this provision with regard to valuation for duty purposes has been in existence for many years. It was there since 1922 I believe, but as I have already stated, it was very rarely invoked. Instead of its application being the exception now, as it was then, it appears to be the general rule so far as the Minister of National Revenue is concerned. It is entirely in the hands of that hon. gentleman, whose ambition in this direction seems to know no bounds. If there were some way of harness-

ing that minister I think it would be a good thing so that there might be some sort of control not only with regard to the regulations but with regard to ministerial orders, which apparently can be got away with. I am not referring so much to the effect in connection with these particular items; I am speaking of a general policy, or rather the excessive use of a policy which was intended not for general application but for application in exceptional circumstances. I am glad to know that the Minister of Finance and his colleagues have on several occasions reversed the decision of the Minister of National Revenue, as in the matter of farm machinery repairs. asked to give the manufacturer another opportunity to soak the consumer a little harder than he has done in the past. speechtext:

He will find that the price of commodities in Canada to-day compares favourably with that of commodities of a similar quality in other countries. If we in this country were to be subject to slaughter competition on the part of countries which manufacture in large quantities and can charge their own people a certain price but, by enlarging their manufacture, can spread their overhead over a larger volume of units, of course we would not survive. But if we prevent that slaughtering under those conditions and enable our own industries to operate to a normal capacity, they can do so 53719-271J	, J
and not increase prices. I assert that in the main, as a result of such protection as has been given in recent years, that has been the experience, and where it has been otherwise we have taken action as, for example, was done in the case of glass.

I have only one objection to what the minister has just said. He speaks of slaughter competition. Representing a rural district and realizing the prices the farmers are to-day receiving for the commodities which they have to sell, I ask: How does the minister expect them to stand quietly by and allow this? At the present time agricultural products must find a place on the markets of the world at slaughter prices; somebody has to take them. When does the price of a commodity become a slaughter price? Wheat to-day, even at the increased price that has existed in the last two or three weeks, is still being sold at distress prices. In the western prairies eggs are being sold at five cents a dozen and dairy butter at eight cents a pound. Are these slaughter prices? How can we afford to buy these manufactured goods? It cannot be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am talking about manufactured products, not agricultural commodities.

But we are receiving slaughter prices for the commodities we have to sell. Why should we not be allowed at some time to buy at slaughter prices? We were told by the party opposite when they were striving to get into power, what they would do for the primary producer, but the position of the latter is very much worse than it was when this government took office. I want to add just one
word to what has already been said. is SI,500,000 which is being imported; I am referring to both British and foreign goods. That certainly cannot increase our manufacturers' capacity 10, 20 or 30 per cent as the minister has pictured.
