speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With the first portion of
the remarks of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth I am not in disagreement. But he must bear in mind this circumstance: if we were dealing with the question of protection for this industry as a thing apart, in view of the fact that to-day we have a tariff board established I would say that his objection was well taken. But at the time we gave increased protection to the woven goods industry we would have given it to the knitted goods industry also but for the fact that we were precluded from doing so by the provisions of the French treaty. Pressure was brought to bear upon the government at that time by the knitted goods industry-I know that my hon. friend from Lisgar will be surprised to hear me say this, but I say so quite frankly- that we should give them the same treatment as was applied to the woven goods industry because of the same needs. They were told at that time that but for the circumstance of the French treaty precluding us from giving them that treatment, they would have received it, and an undertaking was given at that time that if, as and when the French treaty was denounced they would be given the same 
treatment as was given this other class of industry to which I have referred. Therefore it is not unjust that we should carry out our undertaking given at that time despite the fact that to-day we have a tariff board established. One of the provisions of the agreement which we have with Great Britain is that as a matter of right the British manufacturer may appear before the Canadian tariff board in objection to the provisions of our tariff covered by conference agreements or otherwise. It will be competent for them at once to go before the tariff board and deal with these very items, and if there is cause for complaint along the lines indicated by my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth the remedy can be applied. I hope that my hon. friend and the committee will not consider me discourteous when I say that I do not think it is worth while to traverse again the ground that we covered one year and a half and two years ago when similar treatment was meted out to the woven goods industry.
Well worth while.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let us assume for the sake of argument that the contention of my hon. friend from Weyburn is right and that my contention as to what will happen is wrong, that his fears are realized and my hopes are not. The fact remains that the same argument which we held then we hold now with respect to this industry.
Never learned anything?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, we have learned from the experience of the past year and a half that an increase in the tariff does not of necessity involve an increase in the price of goods. On the other hand, to give only one instance-I do not propose to embark on one of those long dissertations upon protection- in the United States, which is the most highly protected country in the world, even in those piping days of prosperity when things were humming, many, many hundreds of articles of manufacture could be obtained cheaper behind the high tariff wall of that country than in most countries of the world, including some free trade countries.
The United States has a big free trade area. '

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, a free trade area behind a tariff wall. We have the same thing in Canada. Our area is larger, but we have not so many people. Having said so much I hope my hon. friends will not expect me to engage again in the kind of discussion that has ob-

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
tained1 hitherto. We only ask with respect to this one item that the same treatment shall be given as was given with respect to other tariff items having to do with the woven goods industry.

The minister was good enough to tell us how many manufacturers were interested in this industry, the number of men employed, the amount of wages paid, and the value of its production for 1931. I wonder if he would give us the same figures for 1929 as to the number of factories, the amount of production, the number of men employed and the amount paid out for labour.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry I have not those facts here, but I think the figures in each case would be much larger for 1929 than for 1931.
The minister says that he has not the figures, but that the amount paid out for labour and the number of men employed would be much larger for 1929 than for 1931.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would assume so.

The minister says he would assume so. A moment ago he was asking for this tariff increase in order to protect this industry and protect the labour employed. Is it not a fact that in 1929 the tariff on these goods was very much lower, and that when that lower tariff was in effect there were more men employed in that industry and more money was paid out for labour?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The answer from my point of view is I think very easy. We are to-day in 1933. If conditions were the same as they were in 1929 there would not be the necessity of asking for this increased' tariff. I think that is the answer, which must be obvious. The conditions throughout the world to-day require different treatment entirely from that which obtained in 1929. My hon. friend says that since then the tariff has been very much increased. That is not so. We had the same tariff until March 21 last on this item as obtained in 1929.
March of a year ago, not last March?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, last March.

Then increasing the tariff is not going to help the industry at all because the minister admits that conditions in the industry are due to conditions in Canada, which I contend are due to the policies of this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On account of world conditions.

It is world conditions to-day, but in 1930 the minister did not say it wa3 world conditions. I heard several Conservatives speakers in Nova Scotia then say that the conditions were entirely due to Canadian policies. The minister said that a number of these manufacturing industries were in the red. Let me tell him that I have some money in one of these industries, and my experience has been that the higher the tariff the less the dividend, and sometimes no dividend. So far as I am concerned I think it would be much better if they were made to stand on their own feet and had to carry on without being bolstered up by the tariff. The minister will never get them out of the red by increasing the tariff. It will simply mean they will da less business.
Take thenr off the bottle.
The minister told me a little while ago that the domestic production was 848,000,000 last year. What was it in 1930 and 1931?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry I have not
those figures here but I shal be glad to get them for my hon. friend. I shall also endeavour to get the figures which my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough asked for.

Would the minister also
bring down information as to the volume as well as the value?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If that is possible.
I should be very glad to get the information.
Carried.
No, it will not carry tonight. This is one of the worst crimes in the whole category.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, surely it will carry tonight. Otherwise we might as well rise.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Let it stand
and go on with something else.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I want to move an amendment widening the item, giving free entry to canvas floats as well as glass floats.

Before the item as amended
passes I would call the minister's attention to the fact that it ought to include the words "sinkers and floats including trawl kegs." A deputation waited upon the minister last year and he assured us that he would keep this in mind when the tariff was adjusted. I have a definite impression-the note I have on it is written by myself, but I certainly got it at the interview-that the minister agreed that sinkers and floats should be exempt from duty under item 682a and promised to keep it in mind for another year. It is the same proposition, and for the same purpose. All that is necessary is to put at the beginning of the item those words: "Sinkers, and floats, including trawl, kegs," and then go on with the words "of aluminum," etc., because then it would apply not only to nets but also to trolling, a very important branch of fishing. The item should read:
Sinkers,- and floats, including trawl kegs of aluminum, glass, cork-
The minister was kind enough to go into it very thoroughly last year, and that was his [DOT]considered opinion at that time. It is all in line with the policy of cheapening the fishermen's means of production.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The item can stand until I look into the matter, but I rise more particularly for the purpose of saying to my hon. friend that if he was under the impression that I gave him any undertaking with respect to what action would be taken concerning an amendment to the tariff, he is entirely in error, because whatever my limitations may be one thing I refrain from doing is to give any intimation as to what amendments will be made to the tariff. All I did was to say that I would give careful thought and consideration to my hon. friend's representations. I may possibly have expressed sympathy with his views, but in no case, either to him or to anyone else, have I said what would be done in respect to a tariff item.

Certainly not; I was misunderstood if I gave that impression. The words I used in this note are that he promised to keep it in mind for another year. I perhaps put my own interpretation on his geniality and the sympathy he exhibited. I

am satisfied that when he does look into it he will see the force of the contention.

It is merely widening the
